United States Travel Service CREATION.-The United States 

Travel Service was established June 

29, 1961, pursuant to the International 

Travel Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 129; 22 

U.S.C. 2121 note) as a primary organization unit in the Department of Commerce.

PURPOSE. The purposes of the 

Travel Service are to develop, plan, and carry out a comprehensive program designed to stimulate and encourage travel to the United States by residents of foreign countries for the purpose of study, culture, recreation, business, and other activities as a means of promoting friendly understanding and good will among peoples of foreign countries and of the United States; encourage the development of tourist facilities, low-cost unit tours, and other arrangements within the United States for meeting the requirements of foreign visitors; foster and encourage the widest possible distribution of the benefits of travel at the cheapest rates between foreign countries and the United States consistent with sound economic principles; encourage the simplification, reduction, or elimination of barriers to travel, and the facilitation of international travel generally; collect, publish, and provide for the exchange of statistics and technical information, including schedules of meetings, fairs, and other attractions, relating to international travel and tourism.

ORGANIZATION.-The program of the Travel Service is conducted by the following divisions: Sales Promotion, Media Relations, Facilitation and 

Planning, and Visitor Services.

In ad-

dition to these divisions, nine overseas offices have been established to stimulate tourist travel. These offices are located in London, England; Paris, France; Frankfurt, Germany; Tokyo, Japan; Sydney, Australia; São Paulo, Brazil; Bogotá, Colombia; and Mexico 

City, Mexico.

ACTIVITIES.-The major share of ap propriated funds are used to provide tools and materials for distribution by the overseas offices, such as advertisements, pamphlets, brochures, posters, slides, and films, in order to help the prospective traveler study and measure the United States against other competitive destinations. 

In addition, the following activities are being carried out: editorial support of the program through domestic and foreign media endorsing the 

United States as a tourist destination; encouragement to State and local community groups for the establishment of "host" services throughout the country; development of ways and means of overcoming barriers to travel; and a study of the economic aspects tourism and patterns of international travel. 

National Bureau of Standards 

(Connecticut Avenue at Van Ness Street NW.; EMerson 2-4040)

The National Bureau of Standards was established by act of Congress of March 3, 1901 (31 Stat. 1449 as amended; 15 U. S. C. 271-286).

The Bureau was initially part of the 

Treasury Department and was transferred to the Department of Commerce and Labor on its creation in 1903. 

PURPOSE.-The fundamental purpose of the National Bureau of Standards is to provide national leadership in the development and use of accurate and uniform techniques of physical measurement. With leadership in physical measurement as the focus, the scientific activity of NBS has three major components: (1) provision of the central basis within the United States of a complete and consistent system of physical measurement, and coordination of that system with the measurement systems of other nations; (2) provision of essential services leading to accurate and uniform physical measurement throughout the Nation's science, industry, and commerce, and consonant with their advancing requirements; and (3) provision of data on the properties of matter and materials which are of importance to science, industry, and commerce, and of which are not available of sufficient accuracy elsewhere. This purpose derives from the statutory responsibility to develop and maintain the national standards for physical measurement, to provide means for their effective utilization, and to determine physical constants and properties of materials of importance to science and industry. Measurement standards are provided for such quantities as length, mass, time, volume, temperature, light, color, electrical energy, radioactivity, X-ray intensity, viscosity, sound, radio frequency, and many others.

The Bureau serves as the contact point of the Federal Government for the exchange of standards with other governments, and participates in developing new and more precise international standards of measurement. 

Also, it provides standards for the States within the United States as they may require and request. 

Additional functions include the development of methods of test, the testing of materials, cooperation with other governmental and private organizations in the establishment of codes and specifications, advisory service to other Government agencies on scientific and technical problems and

21 the invention and development of devices to serve the special needs of these agencies.

The Bureau provides a central Federal technical service in a number of specialized areas, a major example being the operation of the Central Radio 

Propagation Laboratory. 

ORGANIZATION.-The scientific and technical program of the Bureau is conducted by the following divisions:

Analytical and Inorganic Chemistry, Applied Mathematics, Atomic Physics,

Building Research, Circuit Standards, 

Cryogenic Engineering, Data Processing Systems, Electricity, Heat, Inorganic Solids, Ionosphere Research and Propagation, Instrumentation,

Mechanics, Metallurgy, Metrology, 

Physical Chemistry, Polymers, Radio

Propagation Engineering, Radiation 

Physics, Radio Physics, Radio Systems,

Upper Atmosphere and Space Physics, and Weights and Measures. 

The Bureau's radio and cryogenic engineering laboratories are located at 

Boulder, Colo. Various field stations are concerned with radio investigations, with the calibration of railway track scales, and with the testing of materials.

ACTIVITIES.- 

A broad program of fundamental research in in physics, chemistry, mathematics, and engineering is conducted in order to lay the ground work for new standards and to provide means and methods for making comparisons and calibrations with the ever increasing accuracy required by science and industry. Much of this research is directly concerned with the accurate measurement of pure substances and the properties of materials of importance to industry and commerce. 

The testing, calibration, and certification of standards and standard measuring apparatus are a service that the Bureau renders broadly, not only for the Federal Government and State and municipal governments, but also for scientific societies, educational institutions, and firms or individuals engaged in pursuits requiring the use of standards. The testing of products for performance, however, is confined mainly to Federal agencies; for others the Bureau will occasionally do testing if there are no facilities available elsewhere.

Many standards are disseminated most effectively through the preparation and distribution of standard samples of pure substances or industrial materials, the composition and properties of which have been accurately determined.

Advisory functions include consultative services to other Government agencies and dissemination of scientific and technical data through publications and reports, and through technical conferences. In addition to assistance in the preparation of specifications for Federal purchase by agencies of the Government, the Bureau assists States, municipalities, industry, and universities in developing methods of measurement.

The Bureau serves as the coordinating agency to bring together the State officials of weights and measures and other regulatory agencies for national conferences and committee activities, and prepares advisory documents as model codes and digests of existing codes to assist in the formulation of uniform and compatible regulations for building safety, electrical devices, weights and measures, and other regulations related to physical properties. 

Weather Bureau 

(M Street between Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth Streets NW.; telephone, 965-2400)

The national weather service was established in 1870 under the Signal 629590°-62--20 

Corps of the Army. By act of October 

1, 1890 (26 Stat. 653; 15 U. S. C. 311),

the Weather Bureau was organized under the Department of Agriculture, and on July 1, 1891, the weather service was transferred to it from the 

Signal Corps. Subsequent legislation and Executive decisions have greatly increased the Bureau's responsibilities, especially in providing weather service for civil aviation. The President's Reorganization Plan IV transferred the 

Bureau to the Department of Commerce, effective June 30, 1940. 

Weather stations in the Arctic are maintained under authority of the act of May 12, 1946 (60 Stat. 4; 15 U.S.C. 

313a).

The Weather Bureau maintains about 300 offices, manned by full-time personnel, at cities and airports throughout the United States and in 

Puerto Rico and some of the islands of the Pacific Ocean. The local offices of the Bureau make surface and upper air weather measurements required for weather forecasting; maintain records and transmit reports; and where appropriate issue local forecasts and warnings.

In addition, weather reports are made at about 675 other locations by personnel of certain other Government agencies, notably the Federal Aviation

Agency, State and municipal groups, airlines, and private citizens.

Also, the Weather Bureau has approximately 12,000 substations which provide less complex reports and observations to supplement those taken by principal offices. 

For administrative purposes, the supervision of field stations is exercised through 5 regional administrative offices and the Pacific Supervisory

Office. 

In cooperation with the Coast 

Guard, the U.S. Navy, and certain maritime interests, the Weather Bureau maintains ocean weather stations in both the Atlantic and the Pacific and in the Gulf of Mexico.

WEATHER SERVICES.-The Weather 

Bureau maintains a national meteorological center at Suitland, Md., which analyzes weather conditions over the northern hemisphere, prepares guidance prognostic material and disseminates it via facsimile and other rapid communication media to both civil and military forecast offices to support their weather service activities. The.

Severe Local Storm Forecasting Cen ter at Kansas City prepares special forecasts for tornadoes, etc., to augment the radar and volunteer networks maintained by local offices to provide warning service.

A general weather service comprising daily weather bulletins, forecasts, warnings, and advices for the public, agriculture, business, commerce, industry, and other interests is provided through field stations of the Weather Bureau. This information is localized for the area of responsibility assigned to each office, based upon the area forecasts issued from 28 forecast centers. Forecasts are available four times daily to cover weather developments expected during the ensuing 36 to 48 hours. In critical situations warnings of storms and cold waves are issued as conditions warrant, without regard to regular forecasting schedules.

Weather bulletins and forecasts are published by nearly all daily newspapers and broadcast by most commercial radio and television stations in the country. More than 250 radio stations maintain microphones in Weather Bureau offices for direct use by Bureau personnel to make weather information service widely available to the general public. Local communication companies have established Public Service 

Weather Teletypewriter Circuits in about 90 cities of the country for the primary distribution of weather information to mass news disseminators. In turn, the dissemination of this information to the general public is accomplished much more rapidly. The automatic telephone forecast repeater, installed and maintained by the operating telephone company in 12 major cities, has proved a popular service, averaging about 54,000 calls daily per

301: installation with a record of 477,148 calls in one day at one such installation. 

Five-day weather outlook stateoutlook state ments are issued for all parts of the 

United States 3 times weekly. A 30day outlook is issued at Washington twice a month.

The Aviation Weather Service op erates 24 hours every day to supply information and weather forecasts for air operations in the United States and over transocean routes. The domestic service consists of about 250 airport stations, connected by FAA teletypewriter circuits, which collect and exchange detailed reports hourly on weather conditions along the civil airways, and disseminate forecasts and other current weather information. 

Preflight weather briefing is available at all airport stations. Operational forecasts for aviation are issued every 

6 hours by 27 Flight Advisory Weather

Service Centers. Warnings of poten tially hazardous flying weather are issued as needed for safety of aircraft in flight. Also, specially composed pilot weather briefing texts are prepared and transcribed for mass dissemination by continuous, self-repeating broadcast on FAA low frequency air navigation radio channels at 66 locations and on automatic telephone at 44 metropolitan communities over the country. 

Under agreement with foreign governments the Weather Bureau provides forecasts for many overseas air routes.

The international air routes are served by forecasting and pilot briefing services, with special attention to transoceanic and high altitude flights.

These forecasts are disseminated to international airports and interested subscribers by long-line teletypewriter and facsimile circuits. 

A horticultural protection service provides specialized warnings and forecasts on a cooperative basis in certain States where fruit and vegetable production is a major activity. In addition, an agricultural weather service has been established in 8 areas of the country to meet the requirements of farmers for weather information. 

Forecasts, warnings, summaries, and advisories are distributed to mass disseminators in the areas served over a teletypewriter network. An agricultural meteorologist works with research personnel at experiment stations on basic research on agricultureweather relationships and their application to farm operations. The forest fire weather service provides forecasts of humidity, wind, and thunderstorm conditions in the forested regions of the country to assist the United States 

Forest Service and other agencies (State and private) in combating the fire menace. 

The marine meteorological service collects about 1,000 weather observations daily from vessels at sea by radio and supplies bulletins comprising weather reports, forecasts, and storm warnings for broadcasts to ships under way on the oceans and the Great

Lakes. Closely related to this marine work is the hurricane warning service, which issues and distributes its highly important storm advices and warnings from special hurricane forecast centers during the critical seasons.

CLIMATOLOGICAL SERVICES.-Under the guidance of a staff office in Washington, D.C., the Climatological Service collects, publishes, and analyzes data from the 300 regular Weather Bureau stations and the 12,000 substations manned by unpaid cooperative observers. The processing of the data is essentially automated through the operations of three Weather Rec ords Processing Centers at San Fran cisco, Calif., Kansas City, Mo., and 

Chattanooga, Tenn. These centers prepare the observations for publication in regular series which cover the 

United States, Puerto Rico, and the

Trust Territories. The data are available as official evidence on weather conditions in legal cases and insurance settlements.

Analytical work to make the climatological data useful for commerce, industry, and agriculture is carried on at

the National Weather Records Center, 

Asheville, N.C. This Center is equipped with modern electronic data processing facilities. It also acts as the ultimate repository of all United

States weather data, including those collected by meteorological satellites.

Climatological information is disseminated through a field service composed of area and State climatologists.

Their function is developmental work in climatology in cooperation with universities, State organizations, and 

Chambers of Commerce. The field climatologists also collect information on severe storms and cooperate with agricultural agencies in the preparation of weekly weather and crop summaries. These are collected and disseminated nationally through the 

Washington office.

Climatological research is directed toward the charting of all climatic elements, their time trends, the problems of droughts, the average conditions of the upper air, the development of new statistical techniques to assess climatic risks, and the use of climatic data for land use, construction, air conditioning, and air pollution.

HYDROLOGIC SERVICES.--A river and flood forecasting system operates in 90 districts covering all the principal rivers and tributaries of the United 

States. There are 11 river forecast centers or units, each responsible for a major river basin and furnishing key river forecasts to the local district offices within the basin. River stages are observed daily at about 1,300 stations and daily river stage forecasts from 24 to 72 hours in advance are made on many of the larger rivers for the benefit of river navigation and control, in addition to flood stage forecasts made as needed. The observed stages are published in an annual summary for the use of industry, commerce, water utilization, and floodcontrol interests. 

In collaboration with the United 

States Corps of Engineers, the Weather

Bureau maintains and publishes data from a network of some 3,000 special precipitation measuring stations, and makes studies of outstanding storms of record to determine the maximum rainfall amounts likely to fall over river basins for which engineering works are under development. Storm characteristics and frequencies are analyzed for the Department of Agriculture watershed protection program. 

In the Western States the Bureau's network of mountain snowfall stations is used to provide forecasts of runoff from the snow fields for irrigation and other water interests, published from January to May, inclusive, in "Water Supply Forecasts for the Western United States."

METEOROLOGICAL SATELLITE ACTIVI- 

TIES. As a consequence of the unparalleled success of the first several 

TIROS meteorological satellites the 

President, in 1961, requested congressional approval of a plan for the establishment and operation of a National 

Operational Meteorological Satellite 

System which would provide for the continuous observation of worldwide meteorological conditions and for the reporting and processing of the data obtained for use in weather forecasting.

The Weather Bureau has been designated as the managing agency for this system and is proceeding, jointly with the National Aeronautics and

Space Administration, with the construction of Command and Data Acquisition stations, procurement of spacecraft and launch vehicles, and the development and procurement of data processing and communication. systems. Initial operational usage of the system is planned for late 1962 or early 1963 coincident with the launching of the first research and development NIMBUS meteorological satellite by the National Aeronautics and

Space Administration. 

In the interim, the data obtained from the TIROS series of research and development satellites are being used operationally in weather analysis and forecasting.

TH 

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT.-The 

Weather Bureau conducts basic and applied meteorological research in its own laboratories and under contract at universities and other institutions to expand the knowledge of the science of the atmosphere and to improve the services of the Weather Bureau.

Studies are conducted to improve both short-range and extended period forecasts, including research and development work associated with the application of high speed electronic computers in weather forecasting (numerical weather prediction).

Extensive projects for the investigation of both hurricanes and tornadoes are being conducted. The projects include the collection of surface and upper air data from special networks and from aircraft operated for research purposes. These and other data are used in research by the Weather Bureau and at colleges and universities under contract to the Weather Bureau.

Research and development in the field of meteorological instrumentation are being conducted to find new or improved techniques for surface and upper air measurements.

Laboratory and field research is being carried out to obtain a better understanding of the physical processes that bring about condensation and growth of cloud particles to form precipitation. Basic studies are conducted of the cooling and heating of the atmosphere and its large and small scale motions. 

In conjunction with the United

States space program the Weather 

Bureau conducts an expanding program of meteorological satellite research which includes the development of advanced meteorological satellite experiments and analysis of meteorological satellite data with the objectives of developing systems and techniques for maximum utilization of these data in operational weather analysis and forecasting, and of achieving a better understanding of basic atmospheric processes. 

PUBLICATIONS.-Research findings and materials are published in the Research Paper Series and the Monthly 

Weather Review, or in the journals of scientific societies. A variety of periodicals, serials, and miscellaneous publications on weather, climate, and meteorological science is issued to disseminate technical information among meteorologists, climatologists, and the general public, and to make observational data and climatic summaries available to potential users. The periodicals include Daily Weather and 

River Bulletins, Daily Weather Map, Weekly Weather and Crop Bulletin, 

Climatological Data, Storm Data,

Mariners Weather Log, Average Monthly Weather Résumé and Out look, Monthly Weather Review, and

Daily River Stages (annual). The serials include Technical Papers, Research Papers, Hydrometeorological Reports, Observational Manuals, Cli matography of the United States, Ter minal Forecasting Reference Manuals, and Daily Series-Synoptic Weather Maps.

Department of Labor, ninth executive department, was created by act of 

Congress approved March 4, 1913 (37) 

Stat. 736; 5 U. S. C. 611). A Bureau of Labor was first created by Congress in 1884 under the Interior Department. The Bureau of Labor later became independent as a Department of Labor without executive rank. It again returned to bureau status in the De partment of Commerce and Labor which was created by act of February 

14, 1903 (32 Stat. 827; 5 U. S. C. 591).

Additional duties related to the statutory functions of the Department of Labor subsequently have been assigned 

Office of the SECRETARY OF LABOR. -As head of the Department of Labor and the principal adviser to the President in the development and execution of policies and the administration and enforcement of laws relating to wage earners, their working conditions, and their portunities for employment, the Secretary of Labor is charged with the responsibility for all activities of the 

Department of Labor. 

op- 

UNDER SECRETARY OF LABOR.-The 

Under Secretary of Labor is the alternate of the Secretary in the discharge of all the Secretary's responsibilities. 

He serves as Acting Secretary in the 

Secretary's absence.

DEPUTY UNDER SECRETARY OF LA- BOR.-The Deputy Under Secretary assists the Secretary and the Under 

Secretary by reviewing and appraising program operations of the Department, seeing that policies are properly reflected in programs, and that policy objectives are achieved by program operations. He supervises coordination of the mobilization activities of the Department and coordinates all interdepartmental and intradepartmental committee operations of the Department. He supervises the Assistant to the Under Secretary (Field Opera tions) and chairs a Program Operato the Department by new legislation and by Executive order.

PURPOSE.-The Department of La bor is charged, among other things, with administering and enforcing statutes designed to advance the public interest by promoting the welfare of the wage earners of the United States, improving their working conditions, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment.

ORGANIZATION.-All functions of the 

Department are vested in the Secretary of Labor. The structure of the 

Department is shown in the organization chart which appears on page 589. 

Secretary tions and Review Committee composed of the Deputy Assistant Secretaries and the Deputy Solicitor. 

ASSISTANT SECRETARY FOR EMPLOY- MENT AND MANPOWER.-The Assistant Secretary for Employment and Man power has responsibility for the Department's manpower activities, including migratory labor activities. He serves as Executive Vice Chairman of the President's Committee on Equal 

Employment Opportunity and supervises the staff services of the committee.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY FOR INTERNA- TIONAL AFFAIRS.--The Assistant Sec retary for International Affairs has responsibility for the Department's international activities. He directs the 

Bureau of International Labor Affairs and serves as the U.S. member of the governing body of the International 

Labor Organization (ILO), as head of the U.S. delegation to the annual conference of the ILO, and as a mem ber of the Board of Foreign Service. 

ASSISTANT SECRETARY FOR LABOR STANDARDS.—The Assistant Secretary for Labor Standards has responsibility for the Department's activities relating to women and labor standards, and also acts as Director of the Women's 

Bureau.

ASSISTANT SECRETARY FOR LABOR-

MANAGEMENT RELATIONS.-The Assistant Secretary for Labor-Manage ment Relations has responsibility for the Department's labor-management relations activities, including those assigned to the Secretary by Executive order establishing policies governing employee-management cooperation in the Federal service. He also has responsibility for the Department's youth activities. 

THE SOLICITOR OF LABOR.-The So licitor has responsibility for all the legal activities of the Department, for the coordination and preparation of the Department's legislative proposals, reports and testimony on proposed legislation, including executive branch clearances, and for the administration of the Davis-Bacon and related acts except as specifically reserved to the

Secretary. He serves as legal adviser to the Secretary and other officials of the Department.

THE ADMINISTRATIVE ASSISTANT SECRETARY.-The Administrative As sistant Secretary has responsibility for the Department's budgetary and fiscal management, personnel management, administrative management, organization, the Library, and administrative services activities. He is assisted by the 

Deputy Administrative Assistant Sec retary, who serves as the Department's 

Budget Officer and Comptroller, and by the Director of Personnel. 

Office of the Administrative 

Assistant Secretary

The Office of the Administrative As sistant Secretary has responsibility for review, evaluation, and approval of proposed and existing programs in order to determine compliance with departmental plans, policies, and budgetary directives; determination of amounts and adequacy of presentation of budget estimates and apportionments; development, review, and approval of organization structures within the several bureaus; promulgation of regulations and procedures affecting all budget, fiscal, personnel, administrative, management, and service functions; development and maintenance of all major relationships outside the Department on administration and management matters; and coordination of contacts with the Congress, the Bureau of the Budget, and the Civil Service Commission, with the. exception of those involving substantive legislation.

In addition to the foregoing organic responsibilities, the Administrative Assistant Secretary has the following spe cific assignments: Records Adminis trator (including handling and safeguarding defense information); Authentication Officer authorized to perform functions relating to the authentication of material in Department records; member of the Department of 

Labor Incentive Awards Committee, and Award of Merit Committee; 

Chairman, Cafeteria Committee; responsibility for the Department's participation in and planning for all civil defense programs for the protection and safety of the Department's employees; development of all plans for operation of the Department on a decentralized basis in the event of attack or total mobilization; managerial leadership of Department's Automatic

Data Processing (ADP) Program; 

serves as Department of Labor representative on the following interde partmental bodies: Budget Officers' Conference, Executive Officers' Conference, General Services Administra tion Advisory Council, Government 

Services, Inc.; provides for Departmental representation on the Federal 

Supply Board. 

LIBRARY.-The Librarian operates under the direct supervision of the Administrative Assistant Secretary and is responsible for the effective organization and administration of the library services of the Department. The Li brarian approves all purchases of books, newspapers, periodicals, and 2

other publications for the Department in Washington and in the field. 

The Library is a specialized collection of about 405,000 books, periodicals, and pamphlets on labor, and related subjects. It provides reference service to the staff of the Department and to the public, circulates books and periodicals to the staff, and lends material to other libraries. 

Office of Information, Publications, and Reports The Office of Information, Publica tions, and Reports monitors the preparation and distribution of all information dealing with the work of the Department and operates as a departmental clearinghouse for all information of value to labor, business, and to the general public. The Director of 

Information, Publications, and Reports plans and directs all informational activities of the Department, advises the Secretary on the public information aspect of the Department's programs, and develops and maintains appropriate liaison with other agencies and organizations and with foreign countries in connection with the work of the Department. He controls the dissemination of information to the public concerning the Department's activities and programs. He is responsible for adequate distribution of economic, technical, and statistical materials developed by the Department through research and analysis, and for review of materials prepared in the various offices of the Department for conformity with general policy, accuracy, and presentability. The Director supervises departmental relations with press, radio, television, and other public information media. He is clearance officer for all Labor Department releases, and determines the need and suitability of format and style of all informational publications and exhibits planned and prepared in the Department.

Office of Legislative Liaison 

The Director, Office of Legislative 

Liaison, as a Special Assistant to the 

Secretary, is authorized, on behalf of the Secretary and within the general policies established by him, to coordinate, supervise, and direct all legislative activities of the Department, including contacts with the Congress and presentation of Departmental legisla tive programs and views to the Congress.

Office of Manpower, Automation, and Training 

The Office of Manpower, Automa tion, and Training performs functions of the Secretary of Labor under the

Manpower Development and Training Act of 1962 (76 Stat. 23) and the Area Redevelopment Act of 1961 

(75 Stat. 58, 59; 42 U.S.C. 2513, 2514). The Office also coordinates other Department programs and operations relating to manpower planning, development, utilization, distribution, and administration in order to improve the effectiveness of the Department's overall manpower program. Additionally, the Office coordinates manpower development program activities of the Department with those of other Federal, State, and local instrumentalities. as The Office appraises the manpower requirements and resources of the Nation and develops programs, policies, and procedures to deal with the problems of persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment, while considering such factors current and prospective manpower shortages, dislocations in the economy arising from automation or other technological developments, foreign competition, relocation of industry, shifts in market demands, and other changes in the structure of the economy. 

The Office is responsible for planning, directing, coordinating and re viewing Manpower Development Pro-

gram activities authorized under the 

Manpower Development and Training 

Act, and under sections 16 and 17 of the Area Redevelopment Act. This includes determining occupations where reasonable expectation of employment opportunity exists; selecting and referring unemployed workers with potential for training to institutional or on-the-job training programs specifically developed to prepare them for job opportunities previously determined; providing for payment of allowances while in training and counseling and placement services upon completion of training. The Office utilizes the Employment Security 

System of 1800 local public employment offices, working in close coordination with the Bureau of Employment

Security. 

For institutional training, the Secre tary of Health, Education, and Wel fare, upon certification of the need for specific occupational training and the referral of trainees by the Secretary of 

Labor, utilizes the State vocational educational system, or if adequate facilities are not available, makes special arrangements. The Office of 

Manpower, Automation, and Training maintains relationships with the De partment of Health, Education, and 

Welfare to provide such occupational training. 

Office of the President's Committee on Employment of the Handicapped 

The Office of the President's Com mittee on Employment of the Handicapped is established within the Office of the Secretary to provide facilities, staff, and services to the President's

Committee in accordance with the 

President's letters of July 11, 1949, and 

May 10, 1952, and Executive Order 

10994 of February 14, 1962. 

The voluntary citizens committee seeks to create a proper climate in which handicapped men and women workers can seek and find gainful employment suited to their skills and abilities. 

The Committee carries on promotional activities through Governors' committees in all States, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and the District of Columbia. Office of the Solicitor The Solicitor is the chief law officer of the Department of Labor. In such capacity, with the assistance of the 

Deputy Solicitor, he exercises direction and supervision over the legal work of the entire Department. Responsible to him is an immediate staff of assistants and attorneys in Washington and in the field offices of the Department throughout the United States and Puerto Rico. 

The Solicitor is also empowered to perform the duties of the Secretary of 

Labor in certain instances. Pursuant to delegation of authority from the Secre tary, he exercises final authority in the 

Department over the withdrawal of originals and copies of files, records, and documents of the Department, in determining the necessity of publishing documents in the Federal Register, and over tort claims arising out of the Department's activities; performs administrative and interpretative functions under the Davis-Bacon Act and related prevailing-wage statutes, the 

Copeland Act, the Federal Eight-Hour 

Laws, and the functions of the Department under Reorganization Plan 14 of 1950 and the statutes listed in the De partment's Regulations, Part 5 (29 CFR Part 5). 

The Solicitor acts as legal adviser to the Secretary of Labor and to the other administrative officers of the Department. He and attorneys on his staff perform legal services for all bureaus and divisions in the Department.

Bureaus

The Bureau of Apprenticeship and Training (formerly the Apprentice- Training Service and the Bureau of 

Apprenticeship), established in the

Department of Labor under the provisions of an act of August 16, 1937 (50 Stat. 664; 29 U. S. C. 50), was transferred to the Federal Security 

Agency by Executive Order 9139 of 

April 18, 1942. It was transferred to the War Manpower Commission by 

Executive Order 9247 of September 17, 1942, and returned to the Depart ment of Labor by Executive Order 

9617, dated September 19, 1945.

The Bureau provides stimulation, promotion, and technical assistance for the organization of programs to improve and broaden the skills of the work force. Services are provided to industry, management, labor, community groups, and others concerned with manpower development. Bureau activities are carried on in cooperation with State agencies similarly engaged and with vocational education authorities.

Primary emphasis is placed upon promoting the development of skilled craftsmen through apprenticeship. In cooperation with national advisory committees appointed by the Secretary of Labor, the Bureau formulates and recommends fundamentals of apprenticeship for training skilled journeymen in industry. Such fundamentals deal primarily with the welfare of the apprentice as an employed worker and deal with such matters as adequate work experience, length of apprenticeship, provisions for supervision, related technical instruction, wages, hours, working conditions, and employer-employee participation. The 

Bureau, in cooperation with State apprenticeship agencies, endeavors to extend the application of fundamentals of apprenticeship by bringing together employers and labor to formulate programs of apprenticeship, and by giving technical and advisory service to sponsors of such programs. Services are provided for the review of apprenticeship programs and practices and for the registration of apprentices and apprenticeship programs.

Bureau of Employees' Compensation  Bureau of Employees' Compensation, established in the Federal Security Agency under the provisions of section 3 of Reorganization Plan 2, effective July 16, 1946, together with its functions, was transferred to the Department of Labor pursuant to Reorganization Plan 19 of 1950, effective May 

24, 1950.

The Bureau administers the following principal acts: 

1. The Federal Employees' Com pensation Act of September 7, 1916, which provides workmen's compensation benefits for civil officers and employees of the United States who suffer personal injuries while in the performance of duty, includes those who serve without compensation or for nominal compensation, or where acceptance or use of such services is authorized by an act of Congress, or provision is made by law for payment of the travel or other expenses of such person. 

2. The Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act of March 

4, 1927, which provides workmen's compensation benefits for employees in private enterprise while engaged in maritime employment on navigable waters of the United States. 

3. The District of Columbia Work men's Compensation Act of May 17, 1928, extends the provisions of the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act to private employment in the District of Columbia. 

4. The Defense Bases Act of August 

16, 1941, extends, with certain modifications, the provisions of the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' 

Compensation Act to any employment (a) at U.S. military bases in foreign countries, (b) on lands occupied or used by the United States for military purposes outside the continental limits

of the United States, (c) under a contract with the United States for the performance of any public work to be performed outside the continental United States, (d) under certain contracts approved and financed by the United States under the Mutual Security Act of 1954, as amended, (e) in the service of the American employers providing welfare or similar services for the benefit of the Armed 

Forces outside the continental United

States. 

5. The War Hazards Compensation Act of December 2, 1942, provides benefits for persons engaged in the employments listed under the Defense 

Bases Act who suffer injury or death as a result of a war risk hazard, and payments to dependents of employees missing from the place of employment due to the belligerent action of an enemy. 

6. The act of July 26, 1946, pertain ing to the civilian war benefits program. 

7. The War Claims Act of July 3, 

1948, provides benefits to civilian 

American citizens for injury, disability, or death caused by capture or detention by the Japanese Government at 

Midway, Guam, Wake Island, Philippine Islands, or other places subject to Federal jurisdiction, attacked or invaded by the Japanese. 

8. The Outer Continental Shelf 

Lands Act of August 7, 1953, extends the Longshoremen's and Harbor 

Workers' Compensation Act to pro vide compensation for disability or death of an employee resulting from any injury occurring as a result of operations conducted on the Outer 

Continental Shelf, with certain exceptions. 

9. The Nonappropriated Fund In strumentalities Act of July 18, 1958, extends the Longshoremen's and 

Harbor Workers' Act to employees of nonappropriated fund instrumentalities of the Armed Forces, such as Army and Air Force Exchange Service, Army and Air Force Motion Picture 

Service, Navy Ship's Stores Ashore,

Navy Exchanges, Marine Corp Ex changes, Coast Guard Exchanges. 

10. The Federal Employees' Com pensation Act was extended to (a) employees of the District of Columbia

Government, excluding the members of the police and fire departments, (b) members of the military reserve components, (c) members of the Coast Guard Reserve, (d) members of the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps, (e) 

evacuees in the War Relocation 

Camps, (f) persons employed on Federal relief projects created under the provisions of the several federal emergency relief appropriations, (g) com missioned officers of the Public Health 

Service, (h) members of the Civil Air 

Patrol, (i) members of the Reserve 

Officers Training Corps, and (j) other groups. 

The Bureau's director is appointed by the Secretary of Labor. The central office consists of three assistant directors, each of whom is aided by appropriate divisions. Nine district offices administer one or more of the various compensation acts. 

The Bureau is required to determine all questions arising under the Federal 

Employees' Compensation Act. (For provision for review of its decisions, see Employees' Compensation Appeals 

Board.) Among other functions, the 

Bureau is required to determine what. employments come within the scope of the law, whether the injury for which compensation is claimed occurred while in the performance of duty, the period for which compensation may be paid, the amount thereof, and, in case of death, the persons entitled to receive such compensation. 

The Bureau is required to make arrangements to provide prompt and competent medical and hospital services for employees injured in the Federal service, irrespective of the place of their employment.

Under the Longshoremen's and 

Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, the Bureau authorizes insurance

carriers to write insurance to secure the payment of compensation, authorizes employers to act as self-insurers, prepares opinions on questions of law for the guidance of deputy commissioners until such questions are finally settled by judicial determination, and supervises the defense of litigation arising out of this law. Decisions upon claims for compensation under this act, and local supervision of the enforcement of the act, are under deputy commissioners of the Bureau who have jurisdiction within the respective compensation districts to which they are assigned. The decision of the deputy commissioner in respect to a claim for compensation is subject to review by Federal district courts on questions of law. 

All compensation benefits authorized by this law are paid by the employer direct or through his authorized insurance carrier. The cost of administration of this law is paid from a 

Federal appropriation.

Bureau of Employment Security 

The responsibilities of the Bureau of Employment Security relate to the public employment service and the unemployment insurance programs, which are carried out principally under the provisions of the Wagner-Peyser Act, as amended (supplemented by title IV 

of the Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944), titles III, IX, XII, and XV 

of the Social Security Act, as amended, the Federal Unemployment Tax Act, the act of July 12, 1951 (65 Stat. 119), and the Temporary Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1961. 

Title III of the Social Security Act and the Wagner-Peyser Act provide conditions under which a State may receive Federal grants for the administration of its unemployment insurance law and State employment service programs. The latter act imposes certain direct operating duties on the Federal agency, to be carried out through the Bureau's United States 

Employment Service. In addition, there are conditions in the Federal Un employment Tax Act (chapter 23, of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954formerly title IX of the Social Security 

Act) which a State law must meet in order that employers within the State may become entitled to certain credits against the Federal tax for which they are liable under that act. 

Conditions for grants for the administration of State employment offices include a State's acceptance of provisions of the Wagner-Peyser Act and a plan of operation found by the 

Bureau to meet Federal requirements.

In order that a State may receive grants for the administration of its unemployment insurance program, its law must contain a number of provisions required under the Social Security Act. Conditions for approval of 

State unemployment insurance laws for purposes of normal tax offset (credit of State tax paid by an employer against the Federal tax) include provisions for safeguarding workers' rights to benefits and requirements to safeguard benefit funds.

Under the 1960 amendments to the 

Social Security Act, Federal unem ployment tax collections, at the rate of four-tenths of 1 percent of taxable wages, are deposited by the Treasury in the Employment Security Adminis tration Account in the Federal Unem ployment Trust Fund. The costs of 

Federal and State administration of the employment security program are paid from this account after appropriation by the Congress. A Treasury revolving fund was also established to advance funds to the Employment Sec urity Administration Account. 

The 

Federal Unemployment Account in the Unemployment Trust Fund is used to make advances to States whose Trust Fund reserves are inadequate for the payment of benefits. After the balance in the Federal Unemployment Account has reached $550 million or four-tenths of 1 percent of taxable wages, whichever is the greater, and

after the Employment Security Ad ministration Account has a balance of $250 million, excess tax collections will be distributed to the States' accounts in the Unemployment Trust Fund.

The Bureau is also responsible for reviewing operations under the Temporary Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1961 of States signing agreements with the Secretary of Labor for the temporary extension of unemployment compensation to workers exhausting their State benefit rights. The extended benefits are financed by a temporary increase of four-tenths of 1 percent in the tax applicable to covered employers under the Federal Unemployment Tax Act. 

The laws under which the States operate their unemployment insurance programs differ widely in coverage, in benefit provisions, in eligibility and disqualification requirements, and in systems of employer experience rating and the resulting contribution rates.

The Bureau has responsibility for (1) studying and recommending new programs and proposed revision in existing programs relating to the current and anticipated problems and needs of both the wage earner and the employer in the labor market; (2) directly administering employment security programs as required by Federal law, or other delegated authority; (3) keeping abreast of developments in employment security and related fields, and coordinating employment security action with related activities of other bureaus of the 

Department, with other agencies of

Government, and with the public; (4) providing advisory and informational services on employment security matters to the legislative and executive branches of Government; (5) promoting understanding and acceptance of the employment security system; (6) participating in the development of plans, programs, and policies for the mobilization, allocation, and utilization of the civilian labor force under national emergencies; and (8) cooperating with other Federal agencies in providing training and assistance to foreign governments.

The Bureau provides leadership to the State employment security agen cies, involving responsibility to: (1) develop and interpret national policies and goals; (2) study program needs and administrative problems; (3) develop techniques, tools, and measures for improvement in administration and program content; (4) promote adoption of improvements in State legislation and administration; and (5) provide continuing technical assistance and interchange of experi ence and information. Beyond its leadership role, the Bureau obtains and allocates funds necessary for proper and efficient administration of the employment security program in the several States and Territories, conducting audits of related expenditures to insure that funds have been expended for purposes allocated. Also, the Bureau is responsible for insuring con: formity of State laws with requirements of Federal laws, and compliance of State administration with provisions of State laws as necessary to meet Federal legal requirements.

The Bureau's operations cover a wide range of activities. It plans programs on a nationwide basis. To enable sound program planning, it collects and analyzes operational and economic data, which in published form provide Government, labor, management, and the public with information of value in assessing economic trends and developments.

The Bureau conducts evaluations of the administration and operation of 

State employment security agencies. 

This involves the measurement of achievements, the making of recommendations for improving State administrative operations and management, and the provision of assistance in the establishment of improved methods of administration and operation.

Fiscal responsibilities involve justification of appropriation requests before Congress, allocation of funds among States, establishment of standards for expenditures, auditing of State fiscal accounts and records, filing of exceptions on funds improperly expended, review of applicable State laws and their execution, and certification of such laws to enable the allocation of Federal funds for administrative costs.

The Bureau works closely with State agencies in the development and maintenance of a well-selected and trained personnel staff. It develops methods for the selection, training, and management of employment security staff. 

To obtain maximum advantage of the resources available in State employment security agencies, the Bureau coordinates nationwide developmental projects which are designed to provide tools, methods, and material for adaptive use throughout the employment security system. This coordination enables widespread research, testing, and validation of techniques. From such coordinated effort have come such products as the Dictionary of Occupational Titles, occupational tests, and occupational job descriptions. 

The Bureau also actively participates in mobilization planning and in the preparation being made by the Federal Government for national emergencies which might arise. In addition, the Bureau coordinates civil defense and mobilization activities in 

State employment security agencies. 

The eight regional directors of the Bureau whose offices are nearest to those of the Office of Emergency Planning have been designated as the regional directors of the Office of Manpower 

Administration for carrying out the

Department's manpower mobilization activities in the field.

These overall responsibilities are in addition to specific responsibilities for the two basic programs, as described below. 629590°-62- -21 

The Bureau's employment service program responsibilities, as assigned to its United States Employment Service under the provisions of the Wagner- Peyser Act, include assistance in establishing and maintaining systems of public employment offices in the 

States; assistance in coordinating such systems throughout the country and increasing their usefulness by developing and prescribing minimum standards of efficiency; furnishing information as to opportunities for employment and other information of value in operating the systems, including information about labor market developments by area (and classification of areas according to relative labor supply), by industry, by occupation, and for agriculture; maintaining a public employment service for the District of Columbia, a veterans' service devoted to securing employment for veterans, and a farm placement service; and maintaining a system for clearing labor among the 

States. The United States Employ ment Service guides and assists the States in placement functions, occupational analysis, counseling, and testing functions; in maximizing employment opportunities for veterans, older workers, youth, handicapped workers, and members of minority groups; in promoting community efforts toward the greatest possible use of the labor force; in compiling, analyzing, and disseminating labor market information; in promoting use by employers of the public employment service; and in providing materials and techniques to employers for effective use of manpower. Under the Immigration and 

Nationality Act of 1952, the United 

States Employment Service, with the assistance of the State employment security offices, determines that the importation and employment of alien workers will not displace, nor adversely affect the wages and working conditions of, workers in the United States similarly employed.

Within the United States Employ ment Service, special organizational units have been established for maintaining a service for veterans and a service for agricultural workers and employers. The former responsibility (including the assurance of special consideration for veterans and preferential treatment for disabled veterans in employment service activities) is carried out under title IV of the Serv icemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, as amended, and policies established by the Secretary of Labor, through the Veterans Employment Service of the United States Employment 

Service, operating through veterans employment representatives assigned to each of the States and Territories to collaborate with the employment security agency. They have functional responsibility for supervising the registration of veterans in local employment offices and for placing veterans in employment; they assist in obtaining and maintaining current information as to available employment, promote the interest of employers in employing veterans, maintain regular contact with employers and veterans organizations to keep employers informed of veterans available for employment and veterans informed of opportunities for employment, and assist in every possible way in improving work conditions and advancing the employment of veterans.

Responsibility for developing policies and procedures governing the national farm placement program, and for directing and coordinating the activities of that program, is carried out through the Farm Labor Service of the United States Employment Serv ice. The basic functions are to maintain a service for agricultural workers and employers which will provide adequate placement facilities for meeting year-round and seasonal labor requirements of agriculture and related industries; to place individual workers seeking employment in agriculture and related industries, and to provide for the orderly and expeditious seasonal movement of migrant workers to successive jobs by providing place. ment service and current and reliable information regarding crop conditions and employment opportunities. The 

Farm Labor Service also has responsibility for insuring that in the interstate recruitment of farm workers applicable standards are met relating to housing, transportation, and wages.

The Federal Advisory Council on Employment Security, composed of 24

Under

Reorganization Plan 2 of 1949 the 

Council advises the Secretary of Labor and the Director of the Bureau with respect to the administration and coordination of the functions of the Bureau. 

Bureau of International

Labor Affairs 

The Bureau was established on December 31, 1959, replacing the Office of International Labor Affairs orig inally established in 1947. Headed by the Assistant Secretary of Labor for 

International Affairs, the Bureau is principally responsible for discharging 

Department of Labor functions in the international labor field. The Assistant Secretary is also charged with mobilizing, directing, and coordinating all other international activities of the Department's various specialized offices and bureaus. 

These functions and responsibilities of the Bureau include advising on the implications of international labor developments in relation to U.S. foreign and domestic policy, analyzing the impact of domestic policy and developments on labor aspects of foreign affairs, recommending operations designed to promote the United States national interest in the foreign labor field generally and with respect to specific areas of the world, and, with the assistance of other offices and bureaus, operating programs affecting labor which are designed to implement foreign policy. 

The Bureau's staff of geographic area specialists develops detailed action programs in the field of labor for the various foreign countries. Through these country programs, the Government's efforts are coordinated to

achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives as they relate to labor abroad. 

The Department of Labor has pri mary responsibility, under the overall foreign policy guidance of the Department of State, for United States participation in the International Labor

Organization. 

The Bureau also carries out the Department's responsibilities for assisting the Department of State in the management of the Foreign Service, including the labor attaché and Foreign Service labor-reporting programs (the 

Department has statutory membership on the Board of the Foreign Service); for representation on delegations and formulation of labor policy in connection with United States participation in the United Nations Economic and

Social Council and its various commissions; for participation in the Interdepartmental Committee on Trade 

Agreements and the Committee for 

Reciprocity Information; and for participation in the Government's Inter national Trade Fair Program. In these activities the Bureau relies upon technical assistance from other bureaus of the Department.

In the fields of technical cooperation and exchange of persons, the Bureau coordinates and directs programs, both its own and those of other bureaus, which are carried on by the Department under various acts of 

Congress and under administrative agreements with other agencies receiving appropriations for that purpose. 

As requested, consultants are supplied for foreign assignments, technical materials are furnished for use abroad, and training programs are conducted in the United States for foreign nationals. These programs are implemented in cooperation with the Department's bureaus and regional offices, State departments of labor, American trade unions, management, and other private organizations. 

The Bureau's responsibility for advice on the implications of international labor developments in relation to United States foreign and domestic policy calls for a continuing program of area analysis on labor developments in foreign countries. This program, as well as the other international programs of the Department, call for active and current research on foreign labor developments. In this connection, great reliance is placed upon the 

Division of Foreign Labor Conditions of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which is responsible for research on labor around the world.

Bureau of Labor Standards The Bureau of Labor Standards, established by departmental order in 1934, is a service agency to State labor departments and officials, and to labor, employer, and civic groups interested in improving working conditions. The 

Bureau promotes industrial safety and health, develops standards in the field of labor legislation and labor law administration, and in cooperation with the Bureau of International Labor 

Affairs assists in implementing international labor standards. In cooperation with the Bureau of International Labor Affairs, it also carries on programs for international exchange of persons and training.

LEGISLATIVE AND ADMINISTRATIVE STANDARDS.-The Bureau provides technical information and assistance to groups and individuals interested in securing adequate and well administered labor laws. Basic materials are prepared, including summaries of various types of laws and information on the effective administration of labor laws covering a broad field of labor standards. Staff members give technical assistance to State labor departments, management, labor organizations, and civic groups on labor legislation and administration, and in adapting recommended standards and procedures to meet State needs. Governments, international agencies, and interested groups of other countries are provided information on labor law and its administration in this country.

FEDERAL-STATE COORDINATION.- 

Through agreements negotiated by the 

Bureau between Federal and State agencies, the enforcement of wage, hour, industrial home work, child labor, and safety and health laws are coordinated to reduce duplication of inspection and to provide for the most effective use of Federal and State staffs. 

CHILD LABOR AND YOUTH EMPLOY- MENT. The Bureau conducts research and serves as a center of information and advisory service on conditions and programs in the broad field of child labor and youth employment. It develops standards for child-labor regulations and hazardous occupations orders issued by the Secretary of Labor under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and gives advisory service to States on issuance of age certificates accepted under section 3 (1) of the act. It serves as liaison with the Wage and Hour and 

Public Contracts Divisions on child labor matters.

INDUSTRIAL SAFETY STANDARDS.- 

The Bureau assists in developing and promoting standards of industrial safety and health, and providing technical advice and service in that field to State labor departments, labor unions, and trade associations. It serves as headquarters and secretariat for the Federal Safety Council. It carries out activities under the 1958 amendments to the Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Regional office North Atlantic. 

Act, which authorize the Secretary of 

Labor to develop safety and health regulations for the industries, make investigations for compliance, and where necessary enforce the regulations, as well as provide educational and promotional services to insure safe working places. It provides direct consultative safety service to employers and workers subject to the Federal 

Longshoremen's and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act. Upon request, it assists in the preparation of State industrial safety codes, trains State safety personnel, and publishes technical safety bulletins and safety training material. The Bureau cooperates with 

State labor departments in developing and promoting State-wide accidentprevention programs of a continuing nature, on a general or selected industry basis as determined by the States. 

REPORTS AND PUBLIC SERVICE.-The 

Bureau develops and services national, regional, and State conferences essential to the working out of problems of cooperation between Federal and State agencies, and to the activities of the Bureau. It has the responsibility for staffing and servicing the President's

Conference on Occupational Safety, organized in March 1949 at the behest of the President in the interest of reducing the Nation's annual toll of industrial accidents. It prepares publications and processes exhibits and visual material.

Bureau of Labor Statistics 

The Bureau of Labor, the predeces sor of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, was established in the Department of the Interior, by act of June 27, 1884. 

In 1913, after several changes in status, it became the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the newly created Department of Labor. The Bureau is the Govern ment's principal factfinding agency in the field of labor economics, particularly with respect to the collection and analysis of data on employment and manpower, productivity and technological developments, wages, industrial relations, work injuries, prices, and costs and standards of living.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics has no enforcement or administrative functions. Practically all of the basic data it collects from workers, businessmen, and from other governmental agencies are supplied by voluntary cooperation based on their interest in and need for the analyses and summaries which result. The research and statistical projects planned by the Bureau grow out of the needs of these groups, as well as the needs of Congress and the Federal and State governments. 

The information collected is issued in special bulletins and in its official pub lication, the Monthly Labor Review. 

EMPLOYMENT AND THE LABOR 

FORCE. Data are published each month on the labor force, employment, and unemployment, by age, sex, occupation, etc., based on a sample survey of the population. At recurring intervals the surveys provide estimates of the educational attainment of the labor force, the employment of students, family relationship of workers, and other personal and economic characteristics of the labor force.

National estimates are published each month on the employment of wage and salary workers in 365 manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries. In cooperation with State agencies, comparable employment data are provided for all the States and for the more important metropolitan areas. 

Labor turnover rates are provided for 223 industries in manufacturing, mining, and communications. All the Government's current statistics on the labor force, employment, and unem 

Employment and Earnings. 

ployment are published monthly in 

The Bureau conducts studies of trends in unemployment, of problems affecting particular groups in the working population, such as youth and older workers, and prepares analyses and projections of the changing size and dition, the Bureau is responsible for composition of the labor force. In adassessment of the military manpower pool and for projections of potential manpower resources, in relation to requirements under conditions of national emergency.

EARNINGS, WAGES, AND HOURS.- 

Gross average hourly and weekly earnings, and average weekly hours, for production or nonsupervisory workers, are issued currently by the Bureau for about 323 industries on a national basis. Average weekly overtime hours are published currently for 143 manufacturing industry groups. Through the cooperative State program, similar data are made available for all States and the more important metropolitan areas. These statistics are reported monthly in Employment and Earnings.

Occupational wage surveys are made annually in 80 major labor markets.

These studies provide information on the level and distribution of wages and salaries for office clerical, professional and technical, maintenance and power plant, and custodial, warehousing, and shipping occupational categories. 

Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. A more comprehensive national survey of salaries for professional, administrative, technical, and clerical occupations is made annually. 

Occupational wage surveys are made in selected industries covering major manufacturing and nonmanufacturing

industries over a 5-year cycle. A few industries are studied annually; most industries, however, are studied at 3to 5-year intervals. Information is provided on a national and regional basis and for selected areas of concentration. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. 

Distributions of production and related workers and of other nonsupervisory employees by straight-time average hourly earnings are periodically established in studies that provide national and regional estimates for manufacturing and selected nonmanufacturing industries. 

Annual surveys are made in 52 cities of wage rates agreed upon in union contracts for a limited number of occupations in printing and publishing, local streetcar and bus operations, the building trades, and motor trucking. 

Quarterly data are available for 100 cities for seven selected occupations in the construction trades. In

Information on current trends in wage rates and wage practices is presented in a monthly report summarizing current wage settlements. addition, statistical summaries are prepared quarterly and annually. Chronologies showing the historical development of wage rate changes are presented for important bargaining situations in selected industries. A series of indexes of changes in wages and salaries for selected occupational groups are maintained. 

Studies of employer expenditures on selected fringe benefits and of the composition of payroll hours are made over a 3-year cycle in manufacturing and in selected nonmanufacturing industries.

LABOR-MANAGEMENT RELATIONS.- 

The Bureau maintains a file of current union contracts and constitutions which is used as factual background material by unions, employers, and conciliation agencies in the settlement of industrial disputes, and as a guide to the preparation of new agreements. 

The Bureau publishes analyses of union agreements in individual industries and agreement provisions concerning such subjects as vacations, overtime, and grievance procedures. 

Similar studies of health, insurance, and pension plans, and other employee benefit plans and of the substantive provisions of union constitutions are also made. Current statistics on work stoppages resulting from industrial disputes are issued monthly with detailed analyses available annually. The Bureau publishes a biennial Directory of 

National and International Labor 

Unions in the United States, and studies of union membership, structure, and procedures.

PRODUCTIVITY.-The Bureau pub lishes annual indexes of output per man-hour and unit man-hour requirements for the private economy and broad industrial groupings such as manufacturing, mining, and agricul ture. Annual indexes are published comparing trends in productivity with those of employment costs per hour, employment costs per unit of output, and prices for the total private and nonagricultural sector of the economy. 

Indexes are also prepared for selected industries in manufacturing and nonmanufacturing relating output to the man-hours of production workers and of all employees. 

The Bureau conducts studies of technological developments and automation and their implications for productivity and manpower requirements. 

These studies deal with the adjustments made by plants introducing new kinds of equipment, including planning, training, and transfer of workers, the outlook for innovations and for technological developments in different industries, with the projected impact on productivity and changes in number and kind of workers who will be needed.

Studies of the importance of construction in generating employment include estimates for direct, on-site construction activities and for indirect,

3. sto off-site activities such as manufacturing, mining, and transportation. They also provide information on the kind of construction labor used, the timing of construction, and the kinds of materials used. 

INDUSTRIAL HAZARDS AND WORKING CONDITIONS.-The Bureau conducts quarterly surveys on work injuries in manufacturing, and annual surveys in both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing in a large number of industries. 

National estimates are prepared annually for all disabling work injuries, by extent of disability for major industry groups. Special studies are made in industries with high accident rates, to determine accident causes and thereby to stimulate accident prevention programs in the industries studied. 

Technical services are extended to State agencies to assist them in the development of better accident statistics. Currently, State-Federal cooperative injury rate surveys are conducted in 12 States.

PRICES AND COST OF LIVING.-The 

Bureau of Labor Statistics is the principal price-collecting agency of the Federal Government outside the field of agriculture. It has also conducted surveys of goods bought by city workers' families, their family incomes, and their changing standard of living. 

Retail prices are collected regularly in 46 cities for food and for other items such as clothing, housefurnishings, miscellaneous goods and services, and rents. Indexes of consumer prices are published monthly for 5 large cities and quarterly for an additional 15 cities. In addition, a Consumer Price 

Index for the Nation is published monthly.

The Wholesale Price Index includes primary market prices of over 2,000 raw materials, semimanufactured goods, and manufactured goods, divided into 15 major groups, 86 subgroups, and 284 product classes. These data are also classified into 34 indexes by stage of processing, 8 indexes by durability of product, and 27 other special purpose indexes. The Bureau maintains records of over 7,000 price quotations for goods sold in primary markets. Primary market price indexes are published weekly and monthly. 

In addition, the Bureau publishes a daily index of spot market prices. 

Studies of consumers' expenditures are conducted from time to time. The 

Bureau is conducting such a study in about 66 cities during 1961 and 1962 for the purpose of revising the Con sumer Price Index. 

The Bureau's staff renders technical assistance to State and local governments in matters relative to prices and cost of living.

OCCUPATIONAL OUTLOOK.-The Bu reau publishes reports on the longrange employment outlook in important occupations and industries. Data on employment trends, earnings, hours, industrial hazards, collectivebargaining agreements, and technological trends collected by the Bureau are included for guidance purposes, together with information from other

LABOR CONDITIONS IN OTHER COUN- 

TRIES. Basic information and current developments in the labor field in other countries are covered in the Bureau's program. Discussions of the general labor situation in individual countries and summaries of available information on a particular subject in the field of labor economics throughout the world appear in the Monthly Labor Review and in special reports published from time to time in foreign labor reports and bulletins. The Bureau also issues a monthly summary called Labor Developments Abroad. 

International comparisons of labor statistics in general and unit labor costs in particular are also studied and reported on.

In cooperation with the Bureau of 

International Labor Affairs, the Bureau of Labor Statistics provides op portunities for labor statisticians from other countries to study its methods and on request sends consultants to countries undertaking new statistical programs in the labor field.

A further description of the international work of the Bureau of Labor Statistics is found under Bureau of In ternational Labor Affairs. 

Bureau of Labor-Management Reports Me The Bureau of Labor-Management 

Reports was created by departmental order on September 24, 1959, for the purpose of administering and enforcing those provisions of the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 (73 Stat. 519; 29 U.S.C. 401 

note) for which the Secretary of Labor has authority and responsibility. 

Among other provisions, the Labor- 

Management Reporting and Dis closure Act provides for the reporting and disclosure of certain financial transactions and administrative practices of labor organizations and employers; the prevention of abuses in these areas and in the administration of trusteeships by labor organizations; and the enforcement of standards and procedures with respect to the election. and removal of officers of labor organi zations. The act authorizes the Secretary of Labor to conduct investiga tions in the areas that he is responsible for, and to initiate civil and criminal legal actions.
